node.label: Amanda Vickery
node.date_label: “Golden Age to Separate Spheres?” (1993) · The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998) · Behind Closed Doors (2009)
node.description: In “Golden Age to Separate Spheres?” (1993), Amanda Vickery questions recurring accounts of women’s declining power organized around capitalism and separate spheres. The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998) reconstructs genteel Georgian women’s domestic responsibilities and expanding social and intellectual horizons from letters, diaries and accounts. Anna Clark praised the archival interpretation but disputed its characterization of feminist historiography and its proposed alternative. Behind Closed Doors (2009) connects domestic objects and privacy with power, rank and gender. Helen Berry praised its range of evidence while questioning its treatment of solitary devotion and the self. Vickery’s response stresses that access to privacy was unequal and that her book does not date its invention to the Georgian period.
node.representative_figures_and_works: “Golden Age to Separate Spheres? A Review of the Categories and Chronology of English Women’s History” (1993); The Gentleman’s Daughter: Women’s Lives in Georgian England (1998); Gender, Taste, and Material Culture in Britain and North America, 1700–1830 (2006), coedited with John Styles; Behind Closed Doors: At Home in Georgian England (2009); “The Political Day in London, c.1697–1834” (2021), with Hannah Greig.
node.scope_note: The 1993 abstract and selected substantive publisher-displayed notes were read; its main body was not freshly accessible. The 2006 volume was checked through metadata, contents and opening previews; the 2021 article through indexed publisher metadata and extract. proposed_edges.relationship: In “Golden Age to Separate Spheres?” (1993), Vickery endorses key points of Kerber’s 1988 criticism while retaining a stronger focus on social and economic behaviour.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cambridge displayed note 14: “My argument endorses Kerber’s at certain key points.” Note read; article body and Kerber original unread in this dossier.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Golden Age to Separate Spheres?” (1993), Vickery criticizes Davidoff and Hall’s Family Fortunes (1987) for neglecting the gentry; Clark identifies that book as a target of The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary reading is restricted to the substantive authorial comment in Cambridge’s displayed note 53; the article body, including pp. 393–401, was not freshly read. This supports the narrower gentry criticism. Clark’s review, paragraphs beginning “Vickery’s chief target” and “By demonstrating”, supports the 1998 engagement. These parallel edges retain both authors of one jointly authored book; they do not establish two independent exchanges.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewing The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998), Anna Clark praises its archival interpretation but argues that it caricatures feminist historiography and fails to establish a replacement paradigm.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Clark review, lines 40, 51–58 and 90: “does not succeed”. Full review read; book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Clark identifies Vickery’s use of E. P. Thompson’s insight about outward deference and concealed resistance in The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Clark review, line 45: “citing E.P. Thompson’s insight”. Particular Thompson text unidentified; original passages unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewing Behind Closed Doors (2009), Berry compares Vickery’s treatment of British women’s crafts with Ulrich’s earlier intervention in early American historiography.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Berry review, paragraph on chapter nine, browser lines 76–78. Ulrich is printed as “Laura Thatcher Ulrich”; resolved to this run’s Laurel Thatcher Ulrich. No Ulrich title named, no debt or collaboration claimed.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her response concerning Behind Closed Doors (2009), Vickery questions the elite focus of an architectural-privacy narrative associated with Stone, Ariès, Girouard and Heyl.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Author response, browser lines 107–113, especially 109: “the houses and privileges of a tiny elite”. Stone is one of four named exponents. His particular text is unidentified; no sole attribution or fresh Stone reading. Response timestamp inconsistent.

proposed_edges.relationship: “Golden Age to Separate Spheres?” (1993) reopens women’s-history categories and chronologies by comparing recurring narratives of declining power.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cambridge abstract, browser lines 451–453. Abstract and selected substantive notes read; full article body unavailable here. Existing women roster already names Vickery; this adds a direct edge, not a duplicate roster row.

proposed_edges.relationship: Berry places Behind Closed Doors (2009) within the historical turn to consumer behaviour and material culture, crediting its study of interiors and wallpaper with showing that consumer priorities were as much about rank and fortune as about gender.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Berry review, browser lines 43–55, with book locators 3, 125, 259 and 299–304 reported by Berry. Those book pages not independently read. Existing consumption roster preserved.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewing The Gentleman’s Daughter (1998), Linda Colley praises Vickery’s archival achievement but argues that her account of Georgian women’s lives sometimes becomes static and needs fuller consideration of political and social change.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the review’s substantive text on the periodical’s own site. Colley values the book’s close archival work and treatment of household management and possessions, while questioning the extent of change in its narrative and asking how revolutions, war and class conflict affected its subjects. This records a qualified published criticism, not a claim that Colley rejected the book overall or derived her own research programme from it. The page’s bibliographical subtitle is inconsistent with the book’s title; the relationship uses The Gentleman’s Daughter, its unambiguous main title, and its original 1998 year.

proposed_edges.relationship: Vickery’s ‘Golden Age to Separate Spheres?’ (1993) contributed a critical examination of public and private spheres to gender history, a contribution explicitly identified by Jane Whittle and colleagues in The Experience of Work in Early Modern England (2025).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read section 3.5 and note 93 in the publisher’s open chapter. The authors explicitly attribute this conceptual contribution to Vickery, rather than merely including her in a collective reference. Their following discussion uses the scholarship to question assumptions about women’s work, domestic space and observation. The edge records the named contribution to gender history; it does not claim that Vickery founded the field. The original article’s publisher metadata confirms June 1993, distinct from its later online publication. The chapter’s authors are not eligible person endpoints in the supplied endpoint and run-member lists, so no person edges to them are proposed. The existing Vickery–women’s-history pair is preserved; this proposal addresses the separately existing gender-history node.
